title: Numerical Algorithms
body:
We begin our journey into the world of scientific computing. The most basic building block of any numerical computing library is a series of mathematical calculation functions. In this chapter, we introduce implementations of two key mathematical techniques when working with functions: interpolation and integration. We present some key techniques, and show how they are implemented using OCaml, and specifically, how they are supported by mathematical functions provided in the Maths module in Owl.

Running the examples

Source: code/chap02_maths
Run: python3 scripts/run_chapter02.py

In utop, load these teaching modules and follow the examples in order:

OCAML
open Owl;;
#mod_use "/opt/book/code/chap02_maths/book_algorithms.ml";;
#mod_use "/opt/book/code/chap02_maths/book_gaussian.ml";;

These modules contain the teaching implementations shown in this chapter. We use Owl for array operations, special functions and Legendre nodes; the teaching code is maintained separately from Owl’s implementation.

2.1 Interpolation

It is often the case that we do not know the analytical form of a function f, but only some points fi = f(xi) along it. Not knowing the analytical form means that we cannot calculate its precise value f(x) at an arbitrary point x. So we have to estimate f(x) by drawing a smooth curve over the domain of function f. If x is within interval of the given data points xi, i = 1…N, this task is called interpolation; otherwise it is the much more difficult task of extrapolation. In this section, we use OCaml to implement interpolation. The implementation code in this chapter mostly follows the algorithms in the Numerical Recipes book [1].

2.1.1 Polynomial Interpolation

Perhaps the most commonly used interpolation method is polynomial interpolation. Given two points with distinct x-coordinates, exactly one polynomial of degree at most 1 passes through them: a straight line. Similarly, any three points with distinct x-coordinates specify exactly one polynomial of degree at most 2, and so on. Formally, given n points (xi,yi) with distinct xi, i = 1…n, in a two dimensional plane, the interpolating polynomial of degree at most n − 1 through the n points can be expressed using a Lagrange form as shown in Eq. 2.1.

P(x) = ∑ k=1n(∏ j≠ 𝑘 x − xj xk − xj)yk (2.1)

By approximating the unknown function f with such a polynomial, we can then estimate its value at any point.

While straightforward to understand, the implementation of this method turns out to be quite tricky, and also does not provide any estimate of the error in the approximation at a given point. One common implementation uses Neville’s Algorithm [3] which builds up Eq. 2.1 recursively as illustrated in Fig. 2.1. Here Pi(i+1)…(i+m) indicates a polynomial of degree at most m that interpolates across m + 1 points, from i to i + m:

Pi(i+1)…(i+m)(x) = (x − xi+m)Pi(i+1)…(i+m−1)(x) + (xi − x)P(i+1)…(i+m)(x) xi − xi+m (2.2)

For example, suppose we are given 4 points, and we denote a polynomial of degree one that interpolates across two points 0 and 1 by P01, a polynomial of degree 2 that interpolates across three points 0,1,2 by P012, etc. Obviously, P11, or just P1 means a polynomial of degree 0 that goes across point 1. In other words, P1(x) = y1 for any x value. The algorithm’s target is to calculate P0123(x) for a given x value. Eq. 2.2 shows how to combine two parent polynomials into one.

In the implementation, we record the differences between two parents and one child, formally denoted by Cm,i and Dm,i:

Cm,i = Pi…(i+m) − Pi…(i+m−1) Dm,i = Pi…(i+m) − P(i+1)…(i+m) (2.3)

By combining Eq. 2.3 and Eq. 2.2, we can compute the differences at one level (defined by the level m, which involves m + 1 points) using information from the previous level, as shown in Eq. 2.4.

Cm+1,i = (xi − x)(Cm,i+1 − Dm,i) xi − xi+m+1 Dm+1,i = (xi+m+1 − x)(Cm,i+1 − Dm,i) xi − xi+m+1 (2.4)

Thus the core of this algorithm is to start from the initial value of any point, and incrementally increase it by the value of C or D calculated according to Eq. 2.4. The choice of either C or D depends on which route provides the “straightest” update toward the final target. The value of C or D that is added in the last step provides the heuristic error estimate dy. This is not a guaranteed bound on the difference between the interpolant and the unknown function.

The Owl_maths_interpolate module provides a polint function for interpolation and extrapolation. Our teaching implementation, Book_algorithms.polint, has the same interface:

OCAML SESSION
val polint : float array -> float array -> float -> float * float

The function polint xs ys x performs polynomial interpolation based on arrays of points and values xs and ys that constrain the function, plus a given value x, and returns the estimate of the function at that point, f(x), plus an error estimate dy. The implementation, following the algorithm just described, is shown below. As its name suggests, polint approximates complicated curves with the polynomial of the lowest possible degree that intersects the given points.

Neville's Algorithm: OCaml Implementation
OCAML
let polint xs ys x =
  let n = Array.length xs in
  if n = 0 || Array.length ys <> n then invalid_arg "polint: array lengths";
  let c = Array.copy ys in
  let d = Array.copy ys in
  let ns = ref 0 in
  let dy = ref 0. in
  let dif = ref (abs_float (x -. xs.(0))) in

  for i = 0 to n - 1 do
    let dift = abs_float (x -. xs.(i)) in
    if dift < !dif
    then (
      ns := i;
      dif := dift)
  done;

  let y = ref ys.(!ns) in
  ns := !ns - 1;

  for m = 0 to n - 2 do
    for i = 0 to n - m - 2 do
      let ho = xs.(i) -. x in
      let hp = xs.(i + m + 1) -. x in
      let w = c.(i + 1) -. d.(i) in
      let den = ho -. hp in
      assert (den <> 0.);
      let den = w /. den in
      c.(i) <- ho *. den;
      d.(i) <- hp *. den
    done;
    if (2 * !ns) + 2 < n - m - 1
    then dy := c.(!ns + 1)
    else (
      dy := d.(!ns);
      ns := !ns - 1);
    y := !y +. !dy
  done;

  !y, !dy

To see how well this interpolation method works, consider the Gamma special function that we will introduce in Sec. 2.3. This extends the factorial relation y(x) = (x − 1)! to non-integer arguments.

OCAML SESSION
# let xi = [|2; 3; 4; 5; 6|];;
val xi : int array = [|2; 3; 4; 5; 6|]
# let y = Array.map (fun x -> Maths.fact (x - 1)) xi;;
val y : float array = [|1.; 2.; 6.; 24.; 120.|]
# let x = Array.map float_of_int xi;;
val x : float array = [|2.; 3.; 4.; 5.; 6.|]

In this example, we specify five points generated from this factorial function, and see how the approximate function obtained by interpolation compares with the Gamma function itself.

OCAML
let f a = fst (Book_algorithms.polint x y a)

We plot the interpolation function f and compare it to the Gamma function. As can be seen in Fig. 2.2, the interpolated line closely fits the true solution, the Gamma function, within a given domain. However, the fit when extrapolating beyond the given domain, where the x-value falls out of the given data, gets growingly less accurate.

2.1.2 Rational Interpolation

One problem with high-degree polynomial interpolation is that equally spaced nodes can produce large oscillations near the ends of the interval. The code below shows such an example. We choose 11 points equally-spaced on the function f(x) = (1 + x2)−1 (represented by g), and use these points to find an interpolated polynomial (f1).

The Mat module in this code provides a data structure for expressing matrices in Owl. We will introduce this module in Chap. 5. Here we only give a glimpse of the function used in this snippet. The linspace a b n function returns a vector that contains n evenly spaced samples, calculated over the interval [a, b]. The map f m function applies function f to matrix m. The to_array function converts a matrix to an OCaml array. Besides, the scalar_* a m functions apply basic calculation such as add, multiplication, etc. between floating-point number a and the matrix m element-wisely.

OCAML
let a = -5.
let b = 5.
let xs1 = Mat.linspace a b 11
let g x = 1. /. (1. +. x *. x)
let ys1 = Mat.map g xs1
let f1 x =
    let y, _err = Owl_maths_interpolate.polint (Mat.to_array xs1) (Mat.to_array ys1) x in
    y

Fig. 2.3(a) compares functions g and f1. Between the nodes, the interpolating polynomial can change rapidly, especially near the two ends. One solution is to use Chebyshev nodes [7] rather than equally spaced nodes to generate f2, as in the code shown below. Fig. 2.3(b) depicts f2, a much better approximation to the original function g than f1.

OCAML
let xs2 = Mat.linspace 1. 11. 11
let xs2 = Mat.scalar_add
    ((a +. b) /. 2.)
    (Mat.scalar_mul
      ((b -. a) /. 2.)
      (Mat.cos (Mat.scalar_mul (Owl_const.pi /. 11.) (Mat.sub_scalar xs2 0.5)))) |> Mat.reverse
let ys2 = Mat.map g xs2

let f2 x =
    let y, _err = Owl_maths_interpolate.polint (Mat.to_array xs2) (Mat.to_array ys2) x in
    y

However, more often than not, in an interpolation problem, we are not free to choose sample points, and so we may end up with equally spaced nodes no matter what. In such cases Rational Interpolation can be an alternative that gives better results for some functions. A rational interpolation method expresses the interpolation method in the form of the quotient of two polynomials:

R(x) = ∑ i=0a pi xi ∑ j=0b qj xj (2.5)

Here a and b are the numerator and denominator degrees. After fixing the scale of the denominator, there are a + b + 1 free coefficients, so we normally choose a + b + 1 = m for m given points. Similar to the Neville algorithm for polynomial interpolation, a recursive algorithm is proposed by Bulirsch and Stoer [2] to compute Eq. 2.5. Using the same definition as Eq. 2.3, this algorithm starts with one initial y value and iteratively chooses to add the C’s or D’s (the value difference between a child and two parents) step by step. With r = (x − xi)∕(x − xi+m+1), the update rules are shown in Eq. 2.6.

Cm+1,i = rDm,i(Cm,i+1 − Dm,i) rDm,i − Cm,i+1 Dm+1,i = Cm,i+1(Cm,i+1 − Dm,i) rDm,i − Cm,i+1 (2.6)

The OCaml implementation is shown below. It follows a similar structure to the Neville algorithm but with different updating rules.

Implementation of rational interpolation
OCAML
let ratint xs ys x =
  let n = Array.length xs in
  if n = 0 || Array.length ys <> n then invalid_arg "ratint: array lengths";
  match Array.find_index (fun xi -> xi = x) xs with
  | Some i -> ys.(i), 0.
  | None ->
    let c = Array.copy ys in
    let d = Array.map (fun y -> y +. 1e-25) ys in
    let ns = ref 0 in
    for i = 1 to n - 1 do
      if abs_float (x -. xs.(i)) < abs_float (x -. xs.(!ns)) then ns := i
    done;
    let y = ref ys.(!ns) in
    let dy = ref 0. in
    decr ns;
    for m = 1 to n - 1 do
      for i = 0 to n - m - 1 do
        let w = c.(i + 1) -. d.(i) in
        let h = xs.(i + m) -. x in
        let t = (xs.(i) -. x) *. d.(i) /. h in
        let den = t -. c.(i + 1) in
        if den = 0. then failwith "ratint: singular interpolation table";
        let den = w /. den in
        d.(i) <- c.(i + 1) *. den;
        c.(i) <- t *. den
      done;
      if 2 * (!ns + 1) < n - m then dy := c.(!ns + 1)
      else (dy := d.(!ns); decr ns);
      y := !y +. !dy
    done;
    !y, !dy

However, there are still shortcomings in this solution. Points with distinct x-coordinates define a unique interpolating polynomial of bounded degree, but a chosen rational interpolation table can be singular. Moreover, poles can occur where the denominator vanishes without cancellation; values near a pole can become very large.

2.2 Integration

A second key topic in numerical computing is Integration, perhaps one of the most basic tools in any scientist’s toolbox. For example, in Physics, both calculating the displacement of objects given changing velocity and the work done by a force along a path require computing integrals. Given a function f taking a real variable and an interval [a,b] of the real line, the integral of f in this interval is:

∫ abf(x)𝑑𝑥

The result can be viewed as the sum of the signed area of the region in the Cartesian plane bounded by the curve f and the x-axis in the domain [a,b]. The area above the x-axis is positive (adds to the area sum) and that below the x-axis is negative (subtracts from the area sum).

Some integrals can be computed analytically using familiar formulas. For example, ∫ 𝑎 𝑑𝑥 = 𝑎𝑥 + C, ∫ cos⁡(x)𝑑𝑥 = sin⁡(x) + C, ∫ ex𝑑𝑥 = ex + C, and many others. Some integrals are so frequently encountered in certain application areas that their solutions are provided as special functions, and we will introduce some of them in Sec. 2.3. When an analytical expression is unavailable or inconvenient, we use numerical integration. In this section we focus solely on numerical integration methods and their implementation in OCaml.

2.2.1 Basic Algorithms

Owl’s Owl_maths_quadrature module provides several numerical integration routines. Here we use the teaching implementation Book_algorithms.trapz to compute ∫ 14x2𝑑𝑥:

OCAML SESSION
# Book_algorithms.trapz (fun x -> x ** 2.) 1. 4.;;
- : float = 21.0000042915344238

The fundamental theorem of calculus states that:

If f is continuous over the interval [a,b] and F(x) is an anti-derivative of f(x) (i.e. derivative of F equal to f), then ∫ abf(x)𝑑𝑥 = F(b) − F(a).

In this case, we know one such F(x) = x3 3 . 1 We can thus verify this result using this theorem:

∫ 14x2𝑑𝑥 = (43 − 13)∕3 = 21

So you might be thinking, what is this trapz? Using numerical methods (or quadrature) to do integration dates back at least to the invention of calculus. The basic idea is to approximate an integration by summing many small areas under the curve being integrated. There are many algorithms for performing numerical integration, and the trapezoidal rule implemented in trapz is just one of them.

This classical method uses N equally spaced abscissas in [a,b]: x1,x2,…,xN. The area between each pair of adjacent xi and xj is approximated by a trapezoid, and the area formula becomes:

∫ xixj f(x)𝑑𝑥 = h(f(xi) 2 + f(xj) 2 ) + O(h3f″)

The error term O(h3f″) indicates that the approximation error is related to the spacing of the abscissas h and the second order derivative of the original function. The order describes how the error scales with the spacing; for a sufficiently smooth function, the composite trapezoidal rule has error of order h2. Extending this to a sequence of many abscissas, we obtain the extended trapezoidal rule:

∫ x1xN f(x)𝑑𝑥 = h(f(x1) 2 + f(x2) + … + f(xN−1) + f(xN) 2 ) + O((b − a)3f″ N2 ). (2.7)

The function trapz implements the method shown in Eq. 2.7 with the interface:

OCAML SESSION
val trapz :
  ?n:int -> ?eps:float -> (float -> float) -> float -> float -> float

Function trapz ~n ~eps f a b computes the integral of f on interval [a,b] using the trapezoidal rule. The argument n specifies the maximum refinement stage, defaults to 20, and must be between 1 and 25 in this teaching implementation. The convergence threshold eps defaults to 1e-6. We compare successive estimates using 𝚎𝚙𝚜max ⁡ (1,|𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑒|), giving an absolute threshold near zero and a relative threshold for larger values. It works by iterating for several stages, improving the accuracy at each by adding more interior points. The implementation code of trapz is relatively simple, as shown below; it uses the trapzd helper defined next.

Integration Method: Trapezoidal
OCAML
let check_options n eps =
  if n < 1 || n > 25 || eps <= 0. then invalid_arg "quadrature: n or eps"
let converged eps old current =
  abs_float (current -. old) <= eps *. max 1. (abs_float current)

let trapz ?(n = 20) ?(eps = 1e-6) f a b =
  check_options n eps;
  let rec refine stage old =
    let current = trapzd f a b stage in
    if stage = n || (stage > 5 && converged eps old current) then current
    else refine (stage + 1) current
  in
  refine 1 infinity

The core part of this algorithm is the trapzd function that computes the n-th stage of refinement of the extended trapezoidal rule. At the beginning when n = 1, it computes only a rough estimate using the beginning and end of the domain, a and b: b−a 2 (f(a) + f(b)). At each subsequent step n it halves the spacing, adding 2n−2 extra interior points. This simple implementation recomputes the sum at each stage. Its implementation is also straightforward.

OCAML
let trapzd f a b n =
  if n < 1 || n > 25 then invalid_arg "trapzd: stage must be in [1,25]";
  let m = 1 lsl (n - 1) in
  let h = (b -. a) /. float_of_int m in
  let s = ref (0.5 *. (f a +. f b)) in
  for i = 1 to m - 1 do
    s := !s +. f (a +. float_of_int i *. h)
  done;
  h *. !s

Besides applying the trapzd function at each iteration, trapz also checks whether successive estimates differ by less than the threshold specified by eps. This is a stopping rule, not a guaranteed error bound: reaching the stage limit returns the latest estimate even if the test has not passed. Setting an extremely low eps value can also increase errors caused by representing numbers with only finite precision during numerical computation.

Besides trapz, the trapzd method is also a core mechanism in several other integration functions such as Simpson’s Rule. This is similar to trapz in its interface but different in implementation:

∫ x0x2 f(x)𝑑𝑥 = h(f(x0) 3 + 4f(x1) 3 + f(x2) 3 ) + O(h5f(4)). (2.8)

The difference between the Trapezoid method and Simpson’s Rule is illustrated in Fig. 2.4. Compared to the Trapezoid method, Simpson’s rule has a higher order of error, related to the fourth derivative of function f. Rather than approximating the area between each pair of abscissas by a trapezoid, it is approximated by a trapezoid-like shape with one curved (not straight) edge. Its implementation is also similar to the previous method. Extending this to a form similar to Eq. 2.7, it can be shown that:

∫ abf(x)𝑑𝑥 ≈ 4 3S2N −SN 3 , (2.9)

where SN is the composite trapezoidal estimate using N subintervals. Therefore, the Simpson method is often implemented iteratively as follows. The teaching implementation requires at least two stages and uses the same option and convergence helpers as trapz.

Integration Method: Simpson
OCAML
let simpson ?(n = 20) ?(eps = 1e-6) f a b =
  check_options n eps;
  if n < 2 then invalid_arg "simpson: at least two stages";
  let rec refine stage previous_trapezoid previous_simpson =
    let trapezoid = trapzd f a b stage in
    let current = (4. *. trapezoid -. previous_trapezoid) /. 3. in
    if stage = n || (stage > 5 && converged eps previous_simpson current) then current
    else refine (stage + 1) trapezoid current
  in
  refine 2 (trapzd f a b 1) infinity

Another method, Romberg integration (romberg), combines successive trapezoidal estimates to improve accuracy for sufficiently smooth functions. Similar to those methods, it iteratively estimates the integral using more and more intermediate points. The key idea is to use the interpolation method introduced in the previous section to extrapolate trapezoidal estimates to zero spacing. For smooth functions, the error can be expanded in even powers of the spacing, so we interpolate against its square. This goes beyond the single extrapolation step used in Simpson’s method. The teaching implementation uses five successive estimates, including the current stage, and therefore requires at least five stages. The implementation code is shown below and again follows a similar structure to the previous two algorithm implementations.

Integration Method: Romberg
OCAML
let romberg ?(n = 20) ?(eps = 1e-6) f a b =
  check_options n eps;
  let k = 5 in
  if n < k then invalid_arg "romberg: at least five stages";
  let s = Array.make n 0. in
  let h = Array.init n (fun i -> 0.25 ** float_of_int i) in
  let rec refine i =
    s.(i) <- trapzd f a b (i + 1);
    if i + 1 < k then refine (i + 1)
    else (
      let hs = Array.sub h (i - k + 1) k in
      let ss = Array.sub s (i - k + 1) k in
      let result, correction = polint hs ss 0. in
      if i + 1 = n || abs_float correction <= eps *. max 1. (abs_float result)
      then result
      else refine (i + 1))
  in
  refine 0

2.2.2 Gaussian Quadrature

The quadrature methods introduced so far use equally spaced nodes, with weights determined by the particular rule. These methods work well, but it turns out that higher accuracy can be achieved by choosing different and varying weight coefficients and evaluation points. This is the basis of the Gaussian Quadrature method where we approximate ∫ abf(x)𝑑𝑥 with ∑ ⁡ iwif(xi). The weights wi vary with the non-equally spaced evaluation points xi.

Let’s consider an example. Suppose we need to calculate ∫ −11 1 x2+1𝑑𝑥. Basic calculus tells us that the integration result is atan(x)|−11 and so we know the precise integral is:

OCAML SESSION
# atan 1. -. atan (-1.);;
- : float = 1.57079632679489656

How well does a simple left-endpoint rectangle rule perform? For this example, we use 10 abscissas, and the results are shown in the second and third columns of Tbl. 2.1. Using this table, we calculate ∑ ⁡ iwif(xi), where f(x) = 1 x2+1 to obtain the result 1.56746305. Given we used only a small number of abscissas, this is a pretty decent approximation.

Next we apply Gaussian Quadrature using the parameters shown in the fourth and fifth columns in Tbl 2.1. We will discuss these seemingly bizarre parameter choices in a moment. For now, let us calculate ∑ ⁡ iwif(xi) again. Note that these two methods use the same number of abscissas, and the only difference is the choice of weight coefficients and abscissas location. The result should be 1.57079627. Using the unrounded nodes and weights, the absolute error is about 5.7 × 10−8, compared with about 3.3 × 10−3 for the left-endpoint rule. The table shows rounded values; the calculation uses the full-precision nodes and weights.

But what about those curious choices of parameters? They are generated based on something called the Legendre Polynomials, obtained using the gauss_legendre function, as shown in the code below. Notice that these numbers are not affected by the choice of f(x), but only by the upper and lower integration limit and number of abscissas.

OCAML SESSION
# Owl_maths_quadrature.gauss_legendre ~a:(-1.) ~b:1. 10;;
- : float array * float array =
([|-0.973906528517171743; -0.865063366688984536; -0.679409568299024325;
   -0.433395394129247158; -0.148874338981631216; 0.148874338981631216;
   0.433395394129247158; 0.679409568299024325; 0.865063366688984536;
   0.973906528517171743|],
 [|0.066671344308683711; 0.149451349150580531; 0.21908636251528707;
   0.269266719309991742; 0.295524224714752926; 0.295524224714752926;
   0.269266719309991742; 0.21908636251528707; 0.149451349150580531;
   0.066671344308683711|])

The Legendre Polynomials are a system of complete and orthogonal polynomials, with the Legendre polynomial of order n defined iteratively as:

P0(x) = 1 P1(x) = x (n + 1)Pn+1(x) = (2n + 1)xPn(x) − nPn−1(x) (2.10)

In choosing the coefficients in Gaussian quadrature, the xi’s are the roots of the Legendre Polynomials, i.e. those x that make Pn(x) = 0, where n is the number of abscissas. Discussion of the theory behind the Legendre polynomials is beyond the scope of this book; see for example Chapter 4 of Numerical Methods [1] for more information.

Given these Legendre coefficients, the implementation of Gaussian quadrature is not so different from the other previous methods. In our teaching module Book_gaussian, the function gaussian_fixed calculates the quadrature following the procedure shown in the previous example. Note the gauss_legendre_cache array, populated using Owl’s node generator. As the choice of Legendre coefficients is not affected by the specific function used, we can cache previously used parameters for later use, reducing the calculation time. Based on gaussian_fixed, the gaussian function iteratively tests the quadrature result using an increasing number of abscissas, stopping when successive estimates differ by at most eps, or when the maximum number of nodes is reached.

Implementation of Gaussian Quadrature
OCAML
let gauss_legendre = Owl_maths_quadrature.gauss_legendre
let gauss_legendre_cache = Array.init 50 gauss_legendre

let gaussian_fixed ?(n = 10) f a b =
  if n < 1 then invalid_arg "gaussian_fixed: n must be positive";
  let x, w =
    if n < Array.length gauss_legendre_cache then gauss_legendre_cache.(n)
    else gauss_legendre n
  in
  let xr = 0.5 *. (b -. a) in
  let s = ref 0. in
  for i = 0 to n - 1 do
    let c = xr *. (x.(i) +. 1.) +. a in
    s := !s +. w.(i) *. f c
  done;
  !s *. xr

let gaussian ?(n = 50) ?(eps = 1e-6) f a b =
  if n < 1 || eps <= 0. then invalid_arg "gaussian: n or eps";
  let rec refine i old =
    let current = gaussian_fixed ~n:i f a b in
    if i = n || (i > 1 && abs_float (current -. old) <= eps) then current
    else refine (i + 1) current
  in
  refine 1 infinity

In Sec. 2.3 we will introduce several special integral functions that solve particular integrals. One is the sine integral, listed in Tbl. 2.2. As an example, we can compute this integral using Gaussian quadrature to validate its precision. Setting x = 4, the code below shows that numerical method gaussian works well to approximate the true value of the integral.

OCAML SESSION
# let f t = if t = 0. then 1. else sin t /. t;;
val f : float -> float = <fun>
# Book_gaussian.gaussian f 0. 4.;;
- : float = 1.75820313914469306
# Owl_maths.si 4.;;
- : float = 1.75820313894905289

Besides using the Legendre polynomials, the coefficients in Gaussian quadrature can be generated in many other ways including from the Jacobi polynomials, Laguerre polynomials, the Gauss-Hermite quadrature formula, and so on. Again, for more information on these methods, please refer to [1].

2.3 Special Functions

As well as basic mathematical functions from arithmetic, trigonometry, and so on, the Maths module contains a lot of other mathematical functions, important in various fields including mathematical analysis, physics, and so on. The implementations of these functions rely on the Cephes Mathematical Functions Library, a C language library that provides implementation of such functions of interest to scientists and engineers. In the final section of this chapter we briefly introduce some of them, listed in Tbl. 2.2, since you may find them useful from time to time.

The Airy function, named after the British astronomer George Airy contains two linearly independent solutions Ai and Bi to the Airy differential equation. The Maths.airy function accepts a floating-point number x as input, and outputs four floats: Ai, its derivative Ai’, Bi, and its derivative Bi’. One application example is found in problems of quantum mechanics and non-uniform optical wave guides. It is often important to find approximate solutions to linear differential equations with spatially varying coefficients. The Airy function can be used to provide uniform semi-classical approximations in these problems [4].

The Bessel functions were first defined by the mathematician Daniel Bernoulli and then generalised by Friedrich Bessel. In its equation listed in Tbl. 2.2, the complex number α is called the order of the Bessel functions. They are important when studying wave propagation and static potentials, such as electromagnetic waves in a cylindrical waveguide. In solving cylindrical coordinate systems, Bessel functions of integer order or half integer order are often used.

Bessel functions can be divided into two kinds; both solve Bessel’s differential equation. For the non-negative integer orders illustrated here, the first-kind functions remain finite at the origin, whereas the second-kind functions are singular there. A special case is when x is purely imaginary. In this case, the solutions are called the modified Bessel functions, also categorised into both first kind and second kind. These functions are all supported in the Maths module, with names such as j0 (first kind, order 0), j1 (first kind, order 1), and y0 (second kind, order 0), etc.

Both the Airy function and the Bessel function family are solutions to certain differential equations, a topic we will cover in Chap. 6. Fig. 2.5a plots the two solutions Ai and Bi of the Airy function; Fig. 2.5b plots the first kind Bessel function of order 0, 1, and 2. You will notice that they show similar patterns as the solutions to differential equations in Chap. 6.

The Gamma function is widely used in a range of areas such as fluid dynamics, geometry, and astrophysics. It is especially suitable for describing a common pattern of processes that decay exponentially in time or space. The Gamma integral in Tbl. 2.2 converges for Re ⁡ z > 0; the Beta integral requires Re ⁡ x > 0 and Re ⁡ y > 0. The Gamma function extends beyond this region by analytic continuation, with poles at the non-positive integers. The Owl functions used here accept real floating-point arguments. If that input is a positive integer n, the Gamma function simplifies to the factorial function, Γ(n) = (n − 1)!,n ∈𝐙+.

The Gamma function is arguably the most common special function. Its defining integral combines a power with an exponential decay term, a form that occurs in many physical models [5]. In Chap. 3, we will introduce the gamma distribution in statistics, which can be used to model a variety of processes.

In fact, the Gamma function is difficult to avoid even in the definition of other special functions. For example, the Beta function is defined using the Gamma function. Used by Gabriele Veneziano in a paper that wound up marking the beginning of string theory [6], it is also used in the analysis of the preferential attachment process, a type of stochastic urn process that describes how the resource can be distributed among a group of individuals based on the existing resource each one has acquired. The code below illustrates the relationship between the Gamma and Beta functions, and the symmetry of the Beta function, i.e. B(x,y) = B(y,x).

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Maths.beta 3. 4.;;
val x : float = 0.0166666666666666664
# let y = Maths.gamma 3. *. Maths.gamma 4. /. Maths.gamma 7.;;
val y : float = 0.0166666666666666664
# abs_float (Maths.beta 3. 4. -. Maths.beta 4. 3.) < 1e-12;;
- : bool = true

The Error function occurs often in probability and statistics. It is a sigmoid function whose name, error, was proposed due to its connection with the theory of errors in statistics. For a non-negative value x, erf x is the probability that a normal random variable Y with mean μ = 0 and variance σ2 = 0.5 falls in the domain [-x, x]. As it represents a concrete probability, the complementary error function 1 - erf(x) is often also used.

Finally, elliptic integrals are used to find the perimeters of ellipses. The function ellipe m computes the complete elliptic integral of the second kind, E(m), with parameter m. Computing the circumference of an ellipse normally requires integration calculation, but the elliptic integral function provides a ready answer. Suppose an ellipse has semi-major axis a = 4 and semi-minor axis b = 3. With m = 1 − b2∕a2, its circumference can be simply calculated as 4𝑎𝐸(m).

OCAML SESSION
# let a = 4.;;
val a : float = 4.
# let b = 3.;;
val b : float = 3.
# let c = 4. *. a *. Maths.ellipe (1. -. (b /. a) ** 2.);;
val c : float = 22.1034921607095072

As well as the selection we have mentioned, the Maths module provides many other special integral functions including the Dawson integral, Fresnel integral, and Sine integral. They provide alternatives to the basic numerical integration methods we introduced in Sec. 2.2.

2.4 Summary

In this chapter we introduce how to use the mathematical functions in Owl. Specifically, we demonstrated how two important mathematical tools can be implemented in OCaml: interpolation, and integration. We also introduced a selection of important special functions that are provided in the Maths module. The numerical routines in this chapter work with scalar-valued functions and scalar numerical results. Later, in Chap. 5, we will introduce functions whose inputs are N-dimensional arrays, including vectors and matrices.
